newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Fed official wants cut in inflation index.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Fed official wants cut in inflation index.

text.p: The number-two U.S. monetary official on Monday called for a temporary and arbitrary cut in a key measure of inflation, which could shave millions of dollars from government benefit payments.

Federal Reserve Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said politicians should agree to discount the Consumer Price Index (CPI) by about 0.4 percentage point for up to five years when calculating certain benefit increases.

Most economists agree the current CPI overstates the actual increase in the cost of living, but cutting it would be political dynamite, because it is used to set annual increases in Social Security and other government benefits and to set tax brackets.

A commission headed by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin reported last year that the CPI overstated inflation by 1.1 percentage point a year, but Rivlin said she favoured a less-controversial change.

"I would pick a much smaller number like 0.4, so almost no-one could say it was an overestimate of the overestimate, and legislate a temporary reduction in the index," she told a forum sponsored by the Employment Policy Foundation.
She said the temporary change would allow government statisticians time to work on making the CPI a more accurate measure of changes in the cost-of-living.
"I would give the Bureau of Labour Statistics additional resources, considerable additional resources...and a strong mandate to improve the index as much as they can," she said.

Her position was apparently at odds with that of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who said on Jan. 30 that another commission should be created to determine annual cost-of-living increases for federal benefit programmes and tax brackets.

"I just don't think you need it," Rivlin said of the idea. "I think the politicians could sit down and agree on some number which would be quite arbitrary and that's all the commission could do either," she added.
